question: Which statement best describes for?
options: A `for` loop repeats while its condition remains true. It commonly has a starting value, a check, and an update. It is like counting pages until reaching the last one. Make the update move toward the stopping condition to avoid an infinite loop. For example, a for loop can count through the indexes of a short array. In practice, a for loop can visit each index when an item’s position is needed.

`break` exits the current loop; `continue` skips the rest of this repetition and moves to the next one. It is like leaving a queue or skipping one item. Use them when they clarify the logic, but avoid control flow that makes the loop hard to follow. For example, use continue to skip completed records only when that keeps the loop clear. In practice, continue can skip one invalid row while processing later rows.

`for...of` visits each value in an array or another iterable. It is like reading every item from a list in order. Use it when you need the values but not the numeric index. If you need both, another iteration method may make the relationship clearer. For example, use for-of to read each task object when its index is irrelevant. In practice, use for-of to read task objects when their indexes do not matter.

A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is true. It is useful when the number of repetitions is not known in advance. It is like continuing to stir until a mixture reaches the right consistency. Change the condition’s inputs so the loop can finish. For example, a while loop can retry while a response is unavailable, but include a limit or exit. In practice, update the condition’s value inside a while loop so it can stop.
